title: The Platform Is a Product: Lessons from Paved Roads
description: Most internal platforms fail because nobody treated developers as customers. Marisol walks through ten years of paved roads, abandoned portals and one painful rewrite at a fictional logistics company. You will leave with a lightweight product canvas, three metrics that predict adoption, and a checklist for deciding what the platform team should refuse to build.

title: Seeing Inside the Kernel Without Loading Modules
description: Kernel modules are risky, but sometimes the only way to answer why a packet vanished or a syscall stalled. This talk shows how sandboxed programs attached to kernel hooks give you the same visibility with a verifier standing guard. We walk through a real latency investigation on a Kubernetes node and cover the safety model, overhead numbers and the tools worth installing first.

title: Your First Week with Argo CD: Git Push to Pods
description: If your deploys still involve kubectl and crossed fingers, this talk is your gentle on-ramp to GitOps. We start with an empty cluster and a single repository, then install Argo CD, define an Application, and watch drift get corrected automatically. You will see sync policies, health checks and rollbacks explained with plain examples and the three mistakes every newcomer makes.

title: Hands-On eBPF for Absolute Beginners
description: No kernel experience required. In ninety minutes you will write, compile and load your first eBPF programs in a prepared sandbox, counting syscalls, tracing file opens and watching TCP connections as they happen. We explain maps, hooks and the verifier in everyday language, and finish by wiring one probe into a metrics dashboard. Bring a laptop with a browser; everything else is provided.

title: Five Dashboards I Deleted and Why
description: A fifteen minute confession about pretty graphs that never helped anyone during an incident. Nalani shows five real dashboard patterns, why each failed on call, and what replaced them. Expect a ruthless checklist for pruning your own wall of charts, a simple way to tie panels to service level objectives, and a few jokes at the expense of pie charts.

title: AI Agents in Production: What Broke and What Held
description: Three teams that shipped autonomous agents to real users compare notes on the incidents they would rather forget. Topics include runaway tool loops, prompt injection through retrieved documents, cost spikes and evaluation drift. The panel debates when a workflow beats an agent, how to scope tool permissions, and which guardrails survived contact with production traffic. Bring your hardest questions.

title: Hybrid Search with Elasticsearch: Blending Keywords and Vectors
description: Pure vector search misses exact part numbers, while pure keyword search misses intent. Rafaela shows how to combine BM25 and dense embeddings in Elasticsearch using reciprocal rank fusion, and how to tune weights with a small judged query set. We cover index design, embedding model trade-offs, latency budgets and a debugging workflow for answering why that result ranked first.

title: Running PostgreSQL on Kubernetes Without Losing Sleep
description: Stateful workloads on Kubernetes have a reputation, and part of it is deserved. This talk covers operator choices, storage classes, replication topology, connection pooling and the failure modes we hit during a year of running PostgreSQL for a healthcare scheduling product. You will leave with a pre-flight checklist and a sober view of when a managed database is the better answer.

title: Kubernetes Security for Beginners: Locking the Front Door
description: You do not need to be a security specialist to close the most common holes in a cluster. Beatriz explains RBAC, service accounts, pod security standards and secrets handling with small before-and-after manifests. By the end you will have a ten-item hardening checklist, know which defaults are dangerous, and understand how attackers usually get in through misconfiguration rather than exotic exploits.

title: Build a Tracing Pipeline with OpenTelemetry in 90 Minutes
description: Instrument a three-service demo application, run an OpenTelemetry Collector, and follow a single request across process boundaries. You will add manual spans, propagate context through a message queue, sample intelligently, and export traces to an open-source backend. We close with a tour of common pitfalls such as broken context, high cardinality attributes and collectors that quietly drop data.

title: Captions, Contrast, and Keyboards: Accessibility in Developer Tools
description: Terminals, dashboards and documentation sites are used by developers with low vision, motor differences and screen readers, yet they are rarely tested that way. Yasmin demonstrates five accessibility failures in popular tooling patterns and shows quick fixes for each. You will learn how to audit a web UI in fifteen minutes, write meaningful alt text and keep keyboard navigation honest.

title: The Cheapest Node Is the One You Never Started
description: Cloud bills grow quietly, and Kubernetes makes it easy to hide waste behind abstractions. In fifteen minutes Ottoline covers resource requests, bin packing, idle namespaces and spot capacity, with real percentage savings from a mid-sized fleet. Leave with one query to run on Monday and a polite script for talking to teams about their overprovisioned deployments.

title: Mentoring Open-Source Newcomers Without Burning Out Maintainers
description: Good first issues are not enough, and maintainer time is finite. Thaís and Gustavo share a mentoring structure that turned first-time contributors into reviewers across two projects without doubling anyone workload. They cover issue triage templates, office hours, pairing etiquette and how to say no kindly. Bring a project you care about and sketch your own plan during the Q&A.

title: Go Backends That Survive Their First Traffic Spike
description: Your Go service passed every test and still fell over on launch day. Lucian reconstructs three outages caused by unbounded goroutines, missing timeouts and chatty database access, then shows the small changes that fixed them. Expect practical patterns for context cancellation, connection pools, load shedding and profiling with pprof, all illustrated with short code you can copy.

title: Agents Need Guardrails: Designing Software Software Can Use
description: As language models start calling our APIs, every interface becomes an interface for machines with unpredictable judgment. Marguerite argues for narrow tools, explicit budgets, reversible actions and audit trails, drawing on a year of deploying assistants inside enterprise systems. You will leave with a design vocabulary for agent-friendly services and a rubric for deciding what an agent should never be allowed to touch.

title: Model Context Protocol Servers: Design Patterns and Pitfalls
description: Exposing your service through the Model Context Protocol looks easy until a model starts calling it creatively. Anselmo covers tool granularity, schema design, pagination, authentication, error messages that models can actually act on, and testing with recorded conversations. You will see two reference servers built in Go and TypeScript and learn which anti-patterns inflate token costs.

title: Tracing LLM Calls: What to Capture and What to Redact
description: Production AI features fail in ways that logs alone cannot explain: slow retrievals, silent fallbacks and prompts that drift. Odalys shows how to model model calls as spans with OpenTelemetry, which attributes help debugging, and how to redact personal data before it leaves the process. We also cover token cost metrics, sampling strategies and a dashboard layout for on-call engineers.

title: Supply Chain Defense: Signing, SBOMs, and Provenance Hands-On
description: Build a container image, sign it, attach an SBOM, record provenance and enforce all three at admission time in a Kubernetes cluster. You will practice with open tooling in a guided lab, then simulate a poisoned dependency and see which controls catch it. The session ends with a prioritized roadmap for retrofitting these protections into an existing pipeline.

title: Why Your Pre-Commit Hook Is Making Developers Cry
description: A slow hook teaches people to bypass checks, and a bypassed check protects nobody. In fifteen minutes Cosima shows how to profile a local hook chain, move expensive work into CI, and keep only the checks that finish in under three seconds. Expect concrete numbers, a small benchmarking script and a humane policy for hook failures.

title: Cost Is a Feature: FinOps Stories from Kubernetes Fleets
description: Three practitioners describe how they made cloud spend visible without slowing teams down. They compare showback and chargeback, tagging discipline, autoscaler tuning, commitment purchases and the cultural friction of cost conversations. Hear what saved real money, what backfired, and how to pitch efficiency work to leadership who only want new features. Audience questions drive the second half.

title: AI SRE: Letting a Model Triage Your Pager
description: We gave a language model read-only access to metrics, traces and runbooks and let it draft first responses to pages for six months. Fiorella reports hit rates, hallucinated root causes, near misses and the evaluation harness that kept us honest. You will learn how to scope permissions, structure runbooks for machine reading, and decide when a human must stay in the loop.

title: Semantic Search for Support Docs: Lessons from a RAG Rewrite
description: Our support bot answered confidently and wrongly until we rebuilt retrieval from scratch. Matilda explains chunking strategies, metadata filters, embedding choices and the simple evaluation set that exposed the real problems. Beginners will learn how retrieval-augmented generation works end to end, with a minimal Python example and a list of mistakes that waste weeks.

title: Internal Developer Platforms: Golden Paths Versus Golden Cages
description: A golden path accelerates teams, while a golden cage punishes anyone who needs something different. Dimitri shares telemetry from an internal developer platform with four hundred services, showing where escape hatches were used and why. We discuss templates, scorecards, self-service infrastructure and the governance model that let platform engineers say yes more often than no.

title: GitOps Multi-Cluster Rollouts with Argo CD ApplicationSets
description: Manage forty clusters from one repository without copy-paste. In this workshop you generate Applications with ApplicationSets, build a progressive rollout across rings, handle secrets per environment, and practice recovery when a bad change reaches a canary cluster. Prior Argo CD experience is expected, and we spend most of the time debugging realistic failures together.

title: Reviewing Pull Requests with an AI Pair, Without Losing Your Judgment
description: Automated review bots can catch bugs, but they can also flood reviewers with noise and teach teams to ignore comments. Tobias presents data from eight months of an AI reviewer integrated into continuous integration, including precision by comment type. You will learn how to configure severity, keep humans accountable and measure whether review quality improves.

title: Your First Conference Talk: A 15-Minute Survival Kit
description: Nervous about submitting a proposal? Zuleica shares a practical kit built from coaching thirty first-time speakers: writing an abstract that gets accepted, structuring twenty minutes of content, taming slides and rehearsing without a mirror. She also covers handling live demo failures and awkward questions. Bring the half-formed idea in your notes app.

title: WebAssembly Plugins for Platform Teams: Sandboxed Extensions
description: Letting teams extend a gateway or controller usually means running untrusted code in your trusted process. Gwendolyn shows how WebAssembly modules compiled from Rust and Go give you capability-based sandboxing, predictable startup and language freedom. We examine host interface design, resource limits, versioning and the performance numbers from replacing a sidecar fleet with in-process plugins.

title: Threat Modeling Your CI Pipeline
description: Your build system holds the keys to production, yet it rarely gets a security review. Ezequiel walks through a lightweight threat modeling session for a typical pipeline, covering runner isolation, secrets exposure, pull request triggers and third-party actions. You will practice on a sample workflow, leave with a reusable worksheet and learn the quick wins that remove entire attack classes.

title: Open Source Is a Community Before It Is a License
description: Licenses decide what you may do, but people decide whether a project survives. Aurélio draws on fifteen years of maintaining and abandoning projects to describe the unglamorous work that keeps communities alive: governance, kindness, documentation and sustainable funding. The keynote closes with a call to action for companies that depend on volunteers and a short guide for newcomers wanting to start.

title: Kernel-Level Tracing at Scale: Cutting Overhead in eBPF Collectors
description: Running eBPF collectors on ten thousand nodes exposes costs that lab benchmarks hide. Cassiano covers ring buffer tuning, map sizing, in-kernel aggregation, sampling and the verifier limits that shape program design. We look at flame graphs of collector overhead before and after optimization, and share a methodology for deciding which events deserve kernel-side filtering. Familiarity with C or Rust helps.

title: Platform Engineering for Teams of Five
description: You do not need a hundred engineers and a custom portal to have a platform. Noemi describes what a five-person team can reasonably standardize: a deployment template, one observability stack, sensible defaults and a short onboarding document. We discuss what to buy versus build, which Kubernetes features to postpone and how to know when your platform needs to grow.

title: Build an Agentic Incident Responder with Runbooks and MCP
description: Build a working incident helper that reads alerts, queries metrics through MCP servers, follows a runbook and proposes remediation steps for human approval. You will define tools, write evaluation scenarios, add safety limits and replay a simulated outage. The lab uses open models and a sample cluster, so no paid accounts are needed. Expect to leave with a repository you can adapt.

title: A Gentle Introduction to Network Policies
description: By default every pod can talk to every other pod, which is convenient and alarming. In fifteen minutes Luzia demonstrates deny-by-default policies, namespace isolation and egress controls using diagrams and five short manifests. You will learn how to test policies safely, avoid locking yourself out and roll the pattern out across an existing cluster one team at a time.

title: Making Conferences and Code Welcoming for Everyone
description: Organizers and accessibility specialists discuss what actually makes an event or repository welcoming: captioning, step-free venues, quiet spaces, clear codes of conduct and responsive moderation. Panelists share failures from past events, the budget conversations behind improvements and simple changes any maintainer can make today. The audience is invited to contribute practices that worked in their own communities.

title: Evaluating RAG: Measuring Retrieval Before Blaming the Model
description: When a retrieval-augmented system gives wrong answers, teams usually tweak prompts and ignore the index. Henriette presents a measurement-first approach: build judged query sets, track recall at k, inspect chunk boundaries and test rerankers separately from generation. We cover offline and online evaluation, drift detection and cost trade-offs, with examples on both Elasticsearch and PostgreSQL with pgvector.

title: Go Concurrency Patterns for Event-Driven Backends
description: Channels are elegant until a consumer stalls and the whole pipeline backs up. Anders walks through worker pools, bounded queues, fan-in, graceful shutdown and idempotent handlers for a healthcare scheduling backend processing appointment events. Each pattern comes with a failure story, a short Go snippet and a test that reproduces the bug, so you can recognize the same trouble in your own services.

title: Secrets, Sigstore, and the Dependency You Forgot
description: Transitive dependencies and long-lived credentials create quiet paths into production. Teodora dissects a simulated breach that began with an abandoned package and ended with leaked cloud keys, then maps each step to a control: keyless signing, short-lived tokens, dependency pinning and anomaly detection on build behavior. Advanced attendees will appreciate the gritty trade-offs and adoption metrics.

title: Postgres Backups, Failover, and Restore Drills on Kubernetes
description: A backup you have never restored is only a hope. In this workshop you deploy a PostgreSQL cluster with an operator, configure continuous archiving, kill the primary, promote a replica and restore to a point in time. We measure recovery time, discuss replication lag and write a drill schedule your team can actually keep. Comfort with kubectl and basic SQL is assumed.

title: From Alert Fatigue to Signal: Redesigning On-Call
description: Pages at three in the morning for problems nobody can fix are a cultural bug, not a technical one. Marcelina describes how one team cut pages by seventy percent by moving to symptom-based alerts, burn rate thresholds and clear ownership. You will leave with a worksheet for auditing your alerts, a template for post-incident reviews and a sustainable rotation model.

title: Sign Language Interpreters and You: Practical Etiquette for Hosts
description: Working with sign language interpreters is a skill that speakers and organizers rarely get taught. Rosalind covers booking, sharing slides in advance, pacing, positioning, sightlines and how to handle live questions so that deaf attendees are fully included. Fifteen minutes of concrete etiquette that will change how you host, present and plan your next session.

title: Speeding Up CI: Caching, Sharding, and AI-Assisted Test Selection
description: Our pipeline took forty minutes and nobody trusted it. Florian explains how caching layers, test sharding and a machine-learned test selector brought median time to nine minutes, and how we proved the selector did not skip important tests. Expect honest measurements, a flaky test quarantine process and advice on when AI helps with continuous integration and when it only adds complexity.

title: Observing Autonomous Agents: Spans, Costs, and Loops
description: Agents plan, call tools and revise their own work, which makes ordinary request tracing inadequate. Isadora proposes a span model for multi-step reasoning, metrics for loop detection and token spend, and replayable traces for debugging failures. We cover privacy, sampling and building alerts that catch an agent stuck in a loop before the invoice arrives. Experience with tracing systems is assumed.
